idiom_name: collection.iterator.map(..).filter(..).toList - View for deferral, LazyList for memoisation
implementation_notes: Scala's collections provide the lazy realisation: Iterator is a single-pass pull pipeline, View defers every transformer until a strict operation forces it, and LazyList memoises element by element; map/filter/collect/flatMap then compose exactly like filter stages, so the classic Filter/Pipe classes are unnecessary. Because default collection transformers are strict (each step builds a new collection), an idiomatic pipeline starts from .iterator or .view to avoid materialising intermediates. Use Akka/Pekko Streams or fs2 when stages are asynchronous, distributed or demand-driven across threads.
code_sketch:
val report = orders.iterator            // single-pass, lazy
  .filter(_.total > 0)                    // stage 1
  .map(_.withTax(taxRate))                // stage 2
  .collect { case inv if inv.valid => inv }
  .take(1000)
  .toList                                 // one strict operation forces it
pitfalls: Iterators are consumed by the first strict operation; reusing one silently yields an empty result instead of an error.
A View is not a snapshot: it re-reads its base collection, so a captured mutable collection changes under the pipeline, and each traversal repeats the work.
LazyList memoises every evaluated element, so holding one in a val retains its whole computed prefix - use Iterator for one-shot streams.

variants.name: Akka/Pekko Streams linear stages
variants.implementation_notes: Akka Streams - and its Apache-licensed fork Pekko Streams - model the pattern with explicit stages: Source emits, Flow transforms, Sink consumes, and via/to compose a linear (or arbitrary graph) pipeline in which each stage has configurable input/output buffers and backpressure is demand-driven, so a slow sink throttles the whole graph without data loss. Choose it when stages must run asynchronously, at different rates, or across hosts over a stream-aware transport; for in-process transformations the collections pipeline is far lighter and easier to reason about.
variants.code_sketch:
val pipeline: RunnableGraph[Future[Done]] =
  Source(lines)                                     // source
    .via(Flow[String].filter(_.nonEmpty))           // stage 1
    .via(Flow[String].map(Order.parse))             // stage 2
    .toMat(Sink.foreach(sink.write))(Keep.right)    // sink
// pipeline.run()
pitfalls: A stage slower than the graph's demand silently throttles everything upstream; measure per-stage metrics before tuning buffers or adding parallelism.
Failures tear down the whole materialized graph unless a supervision/decider strategy handles them per stage, so a single malformed record can stop the stream.
Materialized values, kill switches and stream completion must be handled explicitly; a stream that is never run does nothing, and one that is not drained leaks resources.
